# GARDEN
## OF THE
# SOUL. <note>original: "Lust-hof des Gemoeds." While "Lust-hof" literally translates to "pleasure-garden," in this religious context it refers to a place of spiritual cultivation and peace. "Gemoed" encompasses the mind, heart, and inner spirit.</note>

### The First CHAPTER.

### How mindfulness <note>original: "aandagtigheid." In 17th-century devotional writing, this refers to a state of focused prayer, spiritual presence, or "attentiveness" to God.</note> must be preserved through the inner approach to God; and the fleeing from the fleeting desires of this world.

There is nothing that grieves us so much as when we do not feel inner devotion, which we lose by turning too much toward things that are outside of ourselves and which cannot help our soul. Therefore the Prophet Isaiah says: *Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which cannot satisfy you?* <note>original: "Esaias." This is a citation of Isaiah 55:2.</note> And he speaks the truth: for what soul was ever satisfied by vanity?

<summary>In this opening chapter, the author introduces the concept of spiritual mindfulness, arguing that focusing on external worldly desires leads to spiritual grief and fails to satisfy the soul's true needs.</summary>

# CHAPTER II.
## How the stillness of the soul is an effective means to approach God, and what harm the flying fantasies cause us.

One might ask / how does one arrive at the point / where one enjoys **God** / and drinks from the **Fountain of Life**? Listen to what **David** said: *My soul is silent before God, who helps me* <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 62:1.</note>. Therefore, whoever wishes to be helped / and to taste the **Fountain** of graces / must first lay aside the worldly desire <term>begeerlykheid</term> <note>In this period, this refers not just to "lust," but to any strong attachment or craving for worldly things that pulls the soul away from God.</note> / through which he is tossed back and forth. This desire arises from fantasies <note>original: "fantasien." In 17th-century spiritual writing, "fantasies" or "imaginations" were seen as distracting mental images and stray thoughts that prevent the mind from being still and focused on the divine.</note> / whose imaginative power is never left idle: but the soul <term>gemoed</term> <note>A Dutch term encompassing the mind, heart, and soul; the seat of emotions and spiritual focus.</note> is drawn into unrest by them / which cannot be overcome except through settling down and stillness / just as one quiets a child that has been troubled by vanity <note>original: "ydelheid." Here meaning frivolous or empty things that over-stimulate a child.</note>. This quieting occurs by presenting something sweet or good / in order to make the lesser thing yield to the greater / or at the very last, the mother’s breasts are given / to make all else forgotten through immediate enjoyment <note>The author uses a nursing metaphor to describe "spiritual tasting" or direct mystical experience, which makes the soul forget worldly distractions.</note>.

### The IV. CHAPTER.

# Of the Threefold Form of Religion: Ceremonial, Opional, and Spiritual: Of Which the Last Encompasses and Includes the First Two.

There is a threefold form of Religion / which we shall depict with three names / namely / <term>Ceremonial</term> <note>original: *Ceremonialis*</note>, <term>Opional</term> <note>original: *Opinionalis*; refers to a faith based on intellectual "opinion" or dogma rather than internal experience.</note>, and <term>Spiritual</term> <note>original: *Spiritualis*</note> / which sometimes exist each individually / sometimes / two together / and sometimes all three together in one person / and these again, with those diverse degrees, are also present within a Congregation. By the Ceremonial, we understand those / who observe the outward institutions of Christ (such as Baptism / the Lord’s Supper / and everything belonging to an outward ministry). Of such was Judas / who served in the Apostolic office and the Deaconship; he also partook of Baptism / the Washing of the Feet / and (as is understood by many) the Lord’s Supper <note>The author uses Judas as the ultimate example of someone who participates in every holy ritual but lacks the internal "Spiritual" component.</note>. ## How the Divine Taste is Found in the Souls Through Good Exercises, of Which the Ancients Also Bore Witness.

# Pleasure-Garden of the Soul. 61

With what a brilliant radiance then **were** these **Philosophers** illumined; indeed it seems no different than how the **Sun** glorifies everything before and after it through its out-thrown rays in a particular way, so that even the heavy clouds become shining and light. In like measure, all that hovered around **Christ**, the **Sun** of righteousness <note>A reference to Malachi 4:2, a biblical prophecy traditionally interpreted by Christians as referring to Jesus Christ.</note>, whether before or after [Him]: the same has been made clear with a special glory. What a cluster of renowned **Men** do we have before the coming of the great dawn, and what a host followed after? How the **Schools** of the **Greeks** swarmed, about three, four, or five hundred years before the time of **Christ**, just after the **Holy Prophets**, like clear-shining **Stars**, had finished their service and set. Immediately here was **Solon** <note>Solon (c. 630 – c. 560 BC), an Athenian lawmaker and poet often counted among the Seven Sages of Greece.</note>, there **Lycurgus** <note>Lycurgus (c. 820 BC), the legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note>, yonder **Pythagoras**, and still further in time **Plato**, **Aristotle**, **Socrates**, **Zeno** <note>Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BC), the founder of the Stoic school of philosophy.</note>, and countless others. It seemed that one hurried and outran the other to deliver his message of the coming light. **Italy** was never so renowned for **Philosophers** and brave **Men** as around the times of **Christ**, being secretly ignited and awakened by the rising **Sun**, as is proven by these presented **Teachings**. # Pleasure-Garden of the Soul. 62

If we wish to cast our eyes upon the **horizon** of the **Christian Teachers**, we shall find the same to be true; for what do we possess through those exceptional lights who are renowned, particularly in the first three, four, or five hundred years after the time of **Christ**? Thus, observing the entire **Heavenly Hemisphere** <note>The 'celestial sphere' or the visible sky as seen from Earth.</note>, we shall find it strewn with countless lights, of which some, like glorious **Planets**, accompany the **Sun**; others, here and there, shine out like **Stars** of the first magnitude; the rest, of lesser size, follow them in good order. Yet the majority, as if hidden in the **Milky Way**, are very far concealed. Finally, casting one's eyes upon the whole work, one shall find it to have been governed by a mighty hand from the time of **Adam** until now, in such a way that nothing but wonder, sweetness, and excellent wisdom is to be noticed therein. Do you not see that children are more moved by one another than by the elderly? In the same way, even though God teaches more powerfully and gives a clearer testimony within the **conscience** <note>Original: "conscientie"—the inner moral compass or the "law written on the heart."</note> and through the **Creation** of all **creatures** <note>Original: "Creaturen"—this refers to all created things (animals, plants, elements), which were seen as a "book of nature" reflecting God’s power.</note>, nevertheless, **human voices** can sometimes stir more movement. Furthermore, whenever the **human voice** testifies to the very same things that God testifies through the **creatures** and in the **conscience**, or speaks through any other means, then those **human voices** may be called **Divine voices**, as they are brought forth by the movement of His **Spirit**. So that, in conclusion, what God is teaching through **Creation**, internally in the **conscience**, and through other means such as visions and audible speech—and through the people whom He moves to that end—it is all the same single word and **teaching**. ### Dialogue of the Wandering Soul

**Wandering Soul.** Could they all fit in there easily?

**Noah.** Very well; for as I have said, the Ark was three hundred cubits <note>original: *ellen*. A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, approximately 18–22 inches.</note> long, fifty wide, and thirty high. When the largest animals were in their places, the small ones took up little room; and the birds, even though there were seven pairs of each, they might well have fit into half of the upper space. One could have placed the small little birds in a space four cubits square; many sat crept under the roof, such as the **Owls** and the **Bats**; others stood on small wooden perches and slept close to one another. Oh! If only a hundred more people had converted, or more, we would have still found room for them; but that wish is in vain, for there was no converting them.

**Wandering Soul.** Father, tell me now how it proceeded.

**Noah.** Oh, Son! Though it makes me sad, I shall nonetheless tell it for your instruction.

**Wandering Soul.** I shall listen eagerly.

**Noah.** On the day that we went into the Ark, it was very beautiful, lovely weather. # Conversation of the Wandering Soul with Noah.

When old Noah had recounted these things, he rose up and went to the eternal rest of the Saints <note>A traditional way of describing the death of a righteous person, entering into heavenly peace</note>. The Wandering Soul also went his way, deeply contemplating within himself everything he had understood from him. And since he had heard many things which he had never read in the Holy Scriptures, nor in any other books in such a detailed form, he wrote those same things in the *Book of Considerations*, and in the *Book of Meditations*, and in the *Book of Diligent Reflections* <note>These titles refer to the Soul's practice of journaling his spiritual journey and thoughts</note>. And because he found nothing in all that he had heard that was in conflict with true history or with reason, he took it all for his own instruction <term>instruction: "leeringe" — providing moral or spiritual guidance</term> and benefit, being inclined to learn even more things to that end.

### Dialogue of the Wandering Soul

...obtained a King; for this reason, Saul—a man of great height—was made the first King over Israel, about four hundred and fifty years after they had departed from Egypt, at the time when Bercillus was King over Assyria, and Codrus was King over Athens. This was about a hundred years after the mighty City of Troy had been destroyed by the Greeks, and the Latin kingdom had been established by Aeneas in Italy; it was also during the beginnings of the kingdoms of Lacedaemonia <note>original: "Lacedemonien"; the region of ancient Greece also known as Sparta.</note> and Corinth.

### Year 3732. With Simeon Cleophas. Book II. 307

He became King in **Syria** in the one hundred and sixty-first year <note>This refers to the Seleucid era, though the events described—the rise of Antiochus IV Epiphanes—historically began around the 137th year of that era (approx. 175 BCE). The author may be using a different chronological reckoning.</note> of the **Greek Empire**. This man, intending to conquer **Egypt** but being forced to retreat by the command of the **Romans**, came to **Jerusalem** with great fury. This city was then wept over by wives and children, for not only did his greedy hands plunder the **Temple** of all its ornament and treasures, but he also shed much blood and filled every street with wretched wailing. His soldiers, far more cruel than **Wild Beasts**, drove their swords through the innocent citizens and slaughtered them like struggling doves. 

But when he had departed for **Antioch** with his plunder, he felt regret that he had not entirely destroyed the city. Therefore, after two years, he sent his Captain **Apollonius** with a mighty army to deliver the same message as before. The citizens trembled and shook when they saw the flying banners before the city gates and heard the sound of the drums. They might have kept him out, but through a **feigned peace** he entered the city on the **Sabbath**. There, the swords were drawn and the spears were leveled. The fleeing, anxious hearts seemed to fly up against the walls in their terror; the echoes of slaughter rang through all the streets, and the blood—

# Book 2. with Simeon Cleophas. III.

# Collation of the Wandering Soul

<note>The "Collation of the Wandering Soul" (Dutch: *De CLXIV Lust-hof der Wandelerende Ziele*) is a famous 17th-century devotional book by Jan Philipsz Schabaelje. It is written as a series of dialogues where a "Wandering Soul" seeks spiritual knowledge from historical figures.</note>

That not one stone should be left upon another / which, however impossible it may have seemed to be / has nevertheless become so desolate in my time / just as you (O Son!) can see today. <note>Simon Cleophas refers to the Roman Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD, which occurred within his lifetime and resulted in the total destruction of the Temple.</note> And going out in the evening / sitting there on the Mount of Olives / he told us all things beforehand / how the City would be besieged / what sorrow / what hardship / what needs would precede it / what misery would arise everywhere in the Land / of hunger / of sorrow / of Pestilences / Wars and Bloodshed / as if I still heard him saying it / with such a significant, serious manner / and piercing words / that they went into our hearts / and they were not in vain: for it happened exactly so / as one can observe today.

**Wandering Soul:** So you sat there until late in the night.

**Sym. Cl.** We have this custom, my Son, that we sometimes come together in the mornings, praising the Lord and pouring out prayers with one another; we also exhort one another to remain steadfast in the faith and to keep ourselves unspotted from the world, thus awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of our Savior Jesus Christ, who shall one day come again, just as we have seen him ascend. To that end, we apply ourselves, so that we may be prepared with a holy walk <term>heylige wandel: a life lived in accordance with religious and moral purity</term>, especially in these times when we do not have a single hour of safety. This is for no other reason than that we proclaim the glad tidings <note>original: "blijde bootschap," referring to the Gospel</note> of the resurrection to all people and forsake the mute idols. # Colloquy of the Wandering Soul

**Authority. S. Cl.** The authority sometimes bears the least blame; this Emperor **Trajan** <note>Trajan (reigned 98–117 AD) was generally regarded by Roman historians as a "good emperor," though early Christian tradition emphasizes the persecutions that occurred under his rule.</note> is otherwise a good man by nature, but is led astray by his priests, just as happened to **Pilate** by **Caiaphas** and his followers. **Therefore,** since this city is the instigator <note>original: "Aenhefster," one who begins or initiates an action</note> of the shedding of innocent blood, the punishments have come entirely upon her neck <note>original: "over den hals gekomen," an idiom meaning to be suddenly overtaken by disaster or a heavy burden</note> like a storm.

**W. S.** Before you proceed further with that subject, tell me first: **What** water do I see lying there so far in the East? It seemed, when the sun rose, that it was all blood because of the reflection of the dawn. Is this a "drowned land" <note>A reference to land lost to the sea, common in Dutch history (verdronken land), here applied to the Dead Sea region.</note> where the dikes have been breached due to war, as sometimes happens?

**S. Cl.** That water, my son, might well have served this city as a warning—yes, as a horrific example of her own destruction—had they paid attention to it. It was once a beautiful, lush land, full of fertile trees, meadows, fields, vineyards, and everything the eye could desire; it also contained finely built cities. For five cities once lay there, full of wanton, wealthy citizens who, out of riches and "bread-drunkenness" <term>brood dronkenheyt: a historical Dutch term for the arrogance and reckless behavior that arises from having too much food and luxury</term>, did not know what mischief they might next commit; moreover...

Cl.</margin> After the burning of the Temple, the remaining Jews, along with the rebellious crowd, fled to one side; and as they would not surrender themselves to the Emperor's mercy, the storming and burning began once again. Thus the Acra Fortress <note>A fortified hilltop structure in Jerusalem, historically a site of great military importance.</note>, the Chancery <note>The administrative office where public records and archives were kept.</note>, the Council House, the magnificent building of Ophel <note>OCR: "Ophlam." There, the fire flew through all the houses; entire streets were licked up into coals. There, one saw all the precious furniture rolling in the ashes; the sealed letters <note>These included deeds of property and legal records, the loss of which meant the destruction of the social and economic order.</note> and the money chests, upon which all their comfort depended, were turned into dust. Many were consumed by the fire, others were suffocated in the smoke, and others were stabbed through, so that the blood, clotting, covered the hot ashes. You must imagine for yourself what a gruesome cry of murder was heard there. The rebels still held the Upper City <note>The western hill of Jerusalem, which was more easily defended due to its height.</note>, which (O Son!) was built upon this mountain. Some wanted to surrender, but Simon bar Gioras <note>OCR: "Simon Giore." A prominent leader of one of the Jewish rebel factions during the First Jewish-Roman War.</note> became aware of this and punished them cruelly; yet, finally, the Romans became masters of the entire city and moved in throngs through the streets to murder and destroy everything they found. There, no one was spared, regardless of what standing or status they held.

### Conference of the Wandering Soul

fortieth year of my age, **Caligula** <note>Emperor Gaius, famously known as Caligula, reigned from 37–41 AD. His reign was marked by increasing tension between the Roman state and the Jewish people.</note> began to reign, under whom the first oppressions against the Jews arose, as well as the persecution of the Apostles. Three years after this, **Claudius** came to the Empire in my fifty-first year, under whom the Gospel writings were begun and the preachers broke out into all places. In my sixty-fifth year, **Nero** began to reign tyrannically, under whom the Holy Apostles were almost all martyred and the destruction of the Jewish land began. **Galba**, **Otho**, and **Vitellius** <note>These three men reigned briefly in rapid succession during the "Year of the Four Emperors" (69 AD) following Nero's suicide.</note> reigned in the eightieth year of my age. After this, **Vespasian** began to reign for ten years, under whom this horrible destruction of the city <note>The Siege and Destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD, which Cleophas and the Wandering Soul are currently witnessing in the form of ruins.</note> occurred, which I have told you of at length, and which you may behold with your own eyes. In my ninetieth year, **Titus** began to reign peacefully, but before three years had ended, his brother **Domitian** began to take up the Empire, who stirred up a fearsome persecution against all Christian assemblies. And in the one-hundred-and-eighth year of my age, **Nerva** began to reign laudably for two years, under whom we had a little rest; but when I had entered my one-hundred-and-eleventh year, the news arrived that a good Emperor, named **Trajan**, had taken the Empire <note>Trajan became emperor in 98 AD.</note>...

<margin>Year 109.</margin> [the Emperor] had reigned, in the beginning of whose reign St. John went to his blessed rest at Ephesus; and this reasonable Emperor <note>Referring to Emperor Trajan (reigned 98–117 AD), often considered one of the "Five Good Emperors" by Romans, though he oversaw localized persecutions of Christians.</note> has, as has been told at length, drawn the sword against us now for eight years; how long it shall yet last is known to Him who knows all things. But I, who have now almost fulfilled the years of Moses <note>In the Bible (Deuteronomy 34:7), Moses lived to be 120 years old. Symeon Cleophas is portrayed here as reaching a similar age.</note>, expect nothing else now but the death of Christ my Lord, so that I may go through that same way to a happy eternity. 

**Wandering Soul:** Oh! That is to be granted to you from the heart, **Father**. I shall long remember your narrative when I see these old delights, these broken passages, those cast-down walls, these mossy stones, those green hills where the foundations of the palaces <note>Original: "Pallepsen," an archaic variant of "paleizen" (palaces).</note> peek out here and there, and especially that high, lofty tower whose top seems to touch the sky; these shall bring to my memory the horrible downfall of this city. This Mount Zion shall make me remember the Kingdom of David; Mount Moriah, the building of the Temple; Mount Calvary, the crucifixion of Jesus; the Mount of Olives, His Ascension; the decayed Bethlehem, His birth; the broken Fountain Gate, His entry; Bethany, His lodging; and furthermore the whole land of His wandering, also

<page-num>588</page-num>
# Collation of the Wandering Soul. #

the journeys, histories, and accounts of the Holy Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles, and all that you have told me at length; but how would I have known what these things were meant to signify, had you, elderly one, not given me complete instruction in everything? Oh! how good it is to hold conversation with wise old people; for not only am I rescued by your narrative from the bewilderment I once felt when I looked upon all these old, decayed structures <note>Original: "Gestigten," referring to buildings or foundations.</note>, but also my understanding has been opened to the entire course of the Divine order. This applies as much to the things that Adam and Noah told me, as to those which I have heard in such good order from your mouth. I have understood the Divine goodness in the fulfillment of His promises, His wisdom, and the acknowledgement of His power in the bringing to naught of the mighty of this world, His justice in the punishment of the wicked, and finally His incomprehensible mercy over those who love and fear Him. Your historical narrative shall be to me like a beautiful clockwork <note>Original: "Horlogie." In this context, it refers to a mechanical timepiece used as a metaphor for the precise, predestined timing of God's plan.</note>, in which all things come to light very precisely in their own time, and the conclusion of which has a very good and desired outcome; it shall be to me...

<meta>Following the conclusion of the dialogue between the Wandering Soul and Simeon Cleophas, this page provides a bibliography of the source materials used to construct the historical and spiritual arguments presented in the preceding "Three Collations" or discourses.</meta>

## These are the Books, from which
### the materials for these three Conversations
### have been drawn.

The Holy Scripture.
Flavius Josephus on the ancient histories and the Wars of the Jews. <note>Josephus was a first-century Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide the primary non-biblical account of the destruction of Jerusalem.</note>
Hegesippus on the destruction of Jerusalem. <note>Hegesippus was an early Christian chronicler; his work survives largely through citations in Eusebius.</note>
Ecclesiastical History by Eusebius. <note>Eusebius of Caesarea is often called the "Father of Church History" for his 4th-century record of the early Church.</note>
Various extracts from Nicephorus. <note>Referring to Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopulus, a 14th-century Byzantine historian.</note>
Ecclesiastical History by Cesare Baronius. <note>A 16th-century Cardinal who wrote the Annales Ecclesiastici in response to Protestant histories.</note>
Augustine in the book "The City of God." <note>original: "De Civitate Dei." This seminal work of Christian philosophy explores the relationship between the earthly and divine realms.</note>
Gaius Pliny on Animals. <note>Referring to the zoological sections of Pliny the Elder’s "Natural History," a foundational Roman encyclopedia.</note>
The Paraphrases of Erasmus. <note>Desiderius Erasmus’s influential plain-language explanations of the New Testament.</note>
The Lessons of Pedro Mexía. <note>original: "Petri Messie." Mexía was a Spanish Renaissance intellectual whose "Silva de varia lección" was a popular collection of history and science.</note>
The Bible of Nature by Du Plessis. <note>Likely referring to Philippe de Mornay, Seigneur du Plessis-Mornay, a French Protestant writer.</note>
The Travel-Book. <note>Likely referring to Heinrich Bünting’s "Itinerarium Sacrae Scripturae," a popular 16th-century guide to biblical geography.</note>
The Biblical Name-Book.
The Low-German Chronology. <note>The term "Low-German" (Nederduytsche) here refers to the Dutch language or the Netherlands region.</note>
The Harmony by John Calvin. <note>A "harmony" is a work that attempts to reconcile the different accounts of the four Gospels into a single narrative.</note>
The Harmony by Gerardus Mercator. <note>While famous as a cartographer, Mercator also wrote a chronological harmony of the Gospels.</note>
The Letter of Lentulus. <note>A famous, though likely apocryphal, document purportedly written by a Roman official describing the physical appearance of Jesus.</note>
The Memorable Sayings.
Various treatises on the Passion.
